title: On slowness as a creative practice
excerpt: What happens when you deliberately resist the pressure to ship, publish, and post — and what you find waiting in the silence.
content: There is a particular kind of anxiety that comes with the modern creative life: the feeling that if you are not producing, you are falling behind. Every day without a post, a tweet, a shipped feature, is a day lost. The feed moves on without you.

I've been trying, deliberately, to move slower. Not out of laziness — I've never worked harder — but out of a suspicion that the pressure to constantly output is quietly destroying the conditions that make good work possible.
Speed optimizes for volume. Slowness optimizes for depth. And depth is what I actually care about.

When I gave myself permission to sit with an idea for weeks instead of days, something changed. The idea stopped being a thing to be processed and became a thing to be understood. I started noticing what I actually thought, rather than what I was supposed to think.

This is not an argument against shipping, or publishing, or being present online. It's an argument for protecting some portion of your creative life from the logic of throughput. For letting some things be slow.

The best work I've done — the pieces I'm most proud of, the projects that held together — all came from periods where I resisted the urge to publish too soon. The silence before the essay is as much a part of the work as the essay itself.
